result:
A deadlock is when two or more threads (or processes, or transactions) each hold a resource the other needs and wait forever for it to be released, so none of them can make progress. The classic case is thread A holding lock 1 and waiting for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1.

It can only happen when four conditions hold at once: resources are exclusive, a thread holds one while waiting for another, a held resource can't be forcibly taken away, and there is a cycle of waiting. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

The most practical fix is to break the cycle by always acquiring locks in the same global order everywhere in the code, so that every thread needing locks 1 and 2 takes 1 first. Where that isn't feasible, acquire with a timeout or try-lock and, on failure, release everything you hold and retry after a short random delay. Beyond that, hold locks for as little time as possible, avoid calling unknown code (callbacks, I/O) while holding one, and prefer a single coarser lock or lock-free designs such as message passing or immutable data when you can.

In databases the same rules apply: touch tables and rows in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and be ready to retry, since the engine will detect a deadlock and abort one of the transactions.
